rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: The HCF of 960 and 432 is :
rows.solution:
\(960 = 2^6 \times 3 \times 5\) and \(432 = 2^4 \times 3^3\).

The HCF takes the lowest power of each common prime: \(2^4 \times 3 = 48\), which is option (A) \(48\).

rows.stem: The natural number 2 is :
rows.solution:
The only factors of 2 are 1 and 2 itself, so 2 is a prime number (the only even prime). It is not composite, since a composite number has a factor other than 1 and itself.

This is option (A) a prime number.

rows.stem: For any natural number \(n\), \(6^n\) ends with the digit :
rows.solution:
\(6 \times 6 = 36\) ends in 6, and multiplying any number ending in 6 by 6 again gives a number ending in 6. So every power \(6^n\) ends with the digit 6.

This is option (B) \(6\).

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is given. The number of zeroes of \(f(x)\) is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the graph of y = f(x) on the XOY axes is the whole question: the number of zeroes is read off the drawing and the stem gives nothing else. Page idx 2.
rows.solution:
The zeroes of \(f(x)\) are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the x-axis. In the figure the whole curve lies above the x-axis and never touches it.

So \(f(x)\) has no zeroes, which is option (A) \(0\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: If a pair of linear equations in two variables is represented by two coincident lines, then the pair of equations has :
rows.solution:
Coincident lines lie one on top of the other, so every point of one line is also on the other. The pair of equations is satisfied by every point on the line.

This is option (D) an infinite number of solutions.

rows.stem: The common difference of the AP : \(\sqrt{2}, 2\sqrt{2}, 3\sqrt{2}, 4\sqrt{2}, \ldots\) is :
rows.solution:
\(d = 2\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}\) (and likewise \(3\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}\)).

This is option (A) \(\sqrt{2}\).

rows.stem: If \(\Delta ABC\) and \(\Delta DEF\) are similar such that \(2\,AB = DE\) and BC = 8 cm, then EF is equal to :
rows.solution:
In similar triangles the corresponding sides are proportional: \(\dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{EF}{BC}\).

\(DE = 2\,AB\), so \(\dfrac{EF}{BC} = 2\) and \(EF = 2 \times 8 = 16\) cm, which is option (D) 16 cm.

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: The mid-point of the line segment joining the points \((5, -4)\) and \((6, 4)\) lies on :
rows.solution:
The mid-point is \(\left(\dfrac{5 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{-4 + 4}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{11}{2}, 0\right)\).

Its y-coordinate is 0, so it lies on the x-axis. This is option (A) \(x\)-axis.

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
rows.stem: Given that \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{a}{b}\), then \(\cos\theta\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
\(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{a^2}{b^2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{b^2 - a^2}}{b}\).

(Equivalently: in a right triangle with opposite side a and hypotenuse b, the adjacent side is \(\sqrt{b^2 - a^2}\).) This is option (C) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2 - a^2}}{b}\).

rows.stem: If \(\cos A = \dfrac{1}{2}\), then the value of \(\sin^2 A + 2\cos^2 A\) is :
rows.solution:
\(\cos A = \dfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(\cos^2 A = \dfrac{1}{4}\) and \(\sin^2 A = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}\).

\(\sin^2 A + 2\cos^2 A = \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{5}{4}\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{5}{4}\).

rows.stem: A car is moving away from the base of a 30 m high tower. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from the car at an instant, when the car is \(10\sqrt{3}\) m away from the base of the tower, is :
rows.solution:
Let \(\theta\) be the angle of elevation. Then \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{30}{10\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}\), so \(\theta = 60^\circ\).

This is option (D) \(60^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: If TP and TQ are two tangents to a circle with centre O from an external point T so that \(\angle POQ = 120^\circ\), then \(\angle PTQ\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
The radii OP and OQ are perpendicular to the tangents, so \(\angle OPT = \angle OQT = 90^\circ\). The angles of the quadrilateral OPTQ add up to \(360^\circ\):

\(\angle PTQ = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ\), which is option (A) \(60^\circ\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, PA is a tangent from an external point P to a circle with centre O. If \(\angle POB = 125^\circ\), then \(\angle APO\) is equal to :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that A, O and B lie on one straight line through the centre, and which angle at O is the marked one, are shown only in the drawing; the stem does not say how B is placed. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
In the figure AB is a diameter, so A, O and B lie on one straight line and \(\angle AOP = 180^\circ - \angle POB = 180^\circ - 125^\circ = 55^\circ\).

The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent PA, so \(\angle OAP = 90^\circ\). In triangle OAP:

\(\angle APO = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 55^\circ = 35^\circ\), which is option (D) \(35^\circ\).

rows.stem: The length of the arc of the sector of a circle with radius 21 cm and of central angle \(60^\circ\), is :
rows.solution:
Length of the arc \(= \dfrac{60}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 = \dfrac{1}{6} \times 132 = 22\) cm.

This is option (A) 22 cm.

rows.stem: The hour hand of a clock is 7 cm long. The angle swept by it between 7:00 a.m. and 8:10 a.m. is :
rows.solution:
The hour hand turns \(30^\circ\) in one hour, that is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) degree per minute. From 7:00 a.m. to 8:10 a.m. is 70 minutes.

Angle swept \(= 70 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 35^\circ\) (the length of the hand does not affect the angle). This is option (C) \(35^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of diameter ‘\(2d\)’ is :
rows.solution:
A diameter of \(2d\) means a radius of \(d\). A solid hemisphere has a curved surface of \(2\pi r^2\) and a flat circular face of \(\pi r^2\).

Total surface area \(= 3\pi r^2 = 3\pi d^2\), which is option (A) \(3\pi d^2\).

rows.stem: If the mean and mode of a data are 12 and 21 respectively, then its median is :
rows.solution:
Use the empirical relation Mode \(= 3\,\)Median \(- 2\,\)Mean:

\(21 = 3\,\)Median \(- 2 \times 12\), so \(3\,\)Median \(= 45\) and Median \(= 15\).

This is option (C) \(15\).

rows.stem: A die is thrown once. Probability of getting a number other than 3 is :
rows.solution:
A die has 6 equally likely outcomes, and 5 of them (1, 2, 4, 5, 6) are numbers other than 3.

\(P = \dfrac{5}{6}\), which is option (C) \(\dfrac{5}{6}\).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The probability that a leap year has 53 Mondays is \(\dfrac{2}{7}\).

**Reason (R) :** The probability that a non-leap year has 53 Mondays is \(\dfrac{5}{7}\).
rows.context: Question numbers 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
A leap year has 366 days, that is 52 complete weeks and 2 extra days. The 2 extra days can be any of 7 equally likely pairs (Sunday-Monday, Monday-Tuesday, ..., Saturday-Sunday), and 2 of these contain a Monday. So the probability of 53 Mondays is \(\dfrac{2}{7}\), and the Assertion is true.

A non-leap year has 365 days, that is 52 weeks and 1 extra day, which is a Monday with probability \(\dfrac{1}{7}\), not \(\dfrac{5}{7}\). So the Reason is false.

The Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The polynomial \(p(y) = y^2 + 4y + 3\) has two zeroes.

**Reason (R) :** A quadratic polynomial can have at most two zeroes.
rows.context: Question numbers 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
\(p(y) = y^2 + 4y + 3 = (y + 1)(y + 3)\), so its zeroes are \(-1\) and \(-3\). The polynomial has two zeroes, and the Assertion is true.

A polynomial of degree 2 has at most 2 zeroes, so the Reason is true. But the Reason only gives an upper limit; it does not show that this polynomial actually has two zeroes (some quadratics have none). That comes from factorising, so the Reason does not explain the Assertion.

Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If \(\alpha, \beta\) are the zeroes of the polynomial \(p(x) = x^2 - 3x - 1\), then find the value of \(\dfrac{1}{\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\beta}\).
rows.solution:
For \(x^2 - 3x - 1\): \(\alpha + \beta = 3\) and \(\alpha\beta = -1\).

\(\dfrac{1}{\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\beta} = \dfrac{\alpha + \beta}{\alpha\beta} = \dfrac{3}{-1} = -3\).

rows.stem: In \(\Delta ABC\), DE \(\parallel\) BC. If AD = \(x\), DB = \(x - 2\), AE = \(x + 2\) and EC = \(x - 1\), then find the value of \(x\).
rows.solution:
DE is parallel to BC, so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\):

\(\dfrac{x}{x - 2} = \dfrac{x + 2}{x - 1}\)

\(x(x - 1) = (x + 2)(x - 2)\), so \(x^2 - x = x^2 - 4\) and \(x = 4\).

(Check: \(AD = 4\), \(DB = 2\), \(AE = 6\), \(EC = 3\), and \(\dfrac{4}{2} = \dfrac{6}{3}\).)

rows.stem: In the figure given above, \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta XYZ\), then find the values of \(x\) and \(y\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - triangles ABC and XYZ drawn side by side; every known side length, and which sides are x and y, is marked only on the drawing. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
From the figure, \(AB = 4\) cm, \(BC = 6\) cm, \(AC = y\), and \(XY = x\), \(YZ = 7.2\) cm, \(XZ = 6\) cm.

\(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta XYZ\), so \(\dfrac{AB}{XY} = \dfrac{BC}{YZ} = \dfrac{AC}{XZ}\), that is \(\dfrac{4}{x} = \dfrac{6}{7.2} = \dfrac{y}{6}\).

\(x = \dfrac{4 \times 7.2}{6} = 4.8\) cm and \(y = \dfrac{6 \times 6}{7.2} = 5\) cm.

rows.stem: The coordinates of the centre of a circle are \((x - 7, 2x)\). Find the value(s) of ‘\(x\)’, if the circle passes through the point \((-9, 11)\) and has radius \(5\sqrt{2}\) units.

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
rows.stem: If \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{24}{7}\), then find the value of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
rows.solution:
\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{24}{7}\): take a right triangle with the side opposite \(\theta\) equal to 24 and the adjacent side 7. The hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25\).

So \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{24}{25}\) and \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{7}{25}\), and

\(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \dfrac{24}{25} + \dfrac{7}{25} = \dfrac{31}{25}\).

rows.stem: If \(\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}\), then find the value of \(\dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)(1 - \sin\theta)}{(1 + \cos\theta)(1 - \cos\theta)}\).
rows.solution:
\(\dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)(1 - \sin\theta)}{(1 + \cos\theta)(1 - \cos\theta)} = \dfrac{1 - \sin^2\theta}{1 - \cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \cot^2\theta\).

\(= \left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{64}\).

rows.stem: Two concentric circles are of radii 5 cm and 4 cm. Find the length of the chord of the larger circle which touches the smaller circle.
rows.solution:
Let O be the common centre and AB the chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle at M.

The radius OM of the smaller circle is perpendicular to the tangent AB at M, so \(OM \perp AB\), with \(OM = 4\) cm and \(OA = 5\) cm.

In right triangle OMA, \(AM = \sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = 3\) cm. The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so \(AB = 2 \times 3 = 6\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: Find the ratio in which the \(x\)-axis divides the line segment joining the points \((-6, 5)\) and \((-4, -1)\). Also, find the point of intersection.
rows.solution:
Let the x-axis meet the segment joining \(A(-6, 5)\) and \(B(-4, -1)\) at \(P(x, 0)\), dividing it in the ratio \(k : 1\). By the section formula

\(P = \left(\dfrac{-4k - 6}{k + 1}, \dfrac{-k + 5}{k + 1}\right)\).

P lies on the x-axis, so \(\dfrac{-k + 5}{k + 1} = 0\), giving \(k = 5\). The ratio is \(5 : 1\).

\(x = \dfrac{-4 \times 5 - 6}{5 + 1} = -\dfrac{26}{6} = -\dfrac{13}{3}\), so the point of intersection is \(\left(-\dfrac{13}{3}, 0\right)\).

rows.stem:
If \(x = h + a\cos\theta\), \(y = k + b\sin\theta\), then prove that :

\(\left(\dfrac{x - h}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{y - k}{b}\right)^2 = 1\)
rows.solution:
\(x = h + a\cos\theta\) gives \(\dfrac{x - h}{a} = \cos\theta\), and \(y = k + b\sin\theta\) gives \(\dfrac{y - k}{b} = \sin\theta\).

So LHS \(= \left(\dfrac{x - h}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{y - k}{b}\right)^2 = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1 =\) RHS.

rows.stem: Prove that : \(\dfrac{\tan A}{1 + \sec A} - \dfrac{\tan A}{1 - \sec A} = 2\operatorname{cosec} A\)
rows.solution:
Write everything in sines and cosines:

LHS \(= \dfrac{\sin A/\cos A}{1 + 1/\cos A} - \dfrac{\sin A/\cos A}{1 - 1/\cos A} = \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A + 1} - \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A - 1}\)

\(= \sin A\left[\dfrac{(\cos A - 1) - (\cos A + 1)}{\cos^2 A - 1}\right] = \sin A\left(\dfrac{-2}{-\sin^2 A}\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{2}{\sin A} = 2\operatorname{cosec} A =\) RHS.

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the given figure, \(\Delta ABC\) is a right triangle in which \(\angle B = 90^\circ\), AB = 4 cm and BC = 3 cm. Find the radius of the circle inscribed in the triangle ABC.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - right triangle ABC (right angle at B) with its incircle drawn; the stem states every value and the configuration. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
\(AC = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\) cm.

Let the circle, with centre O, touch AB at D, BC at E and AC at F, and let \(BD = BE = x\) cm (tangents from B are equal).

Then \(AD = 4 - x\) and \(CE = 3 - x\). Tangents from A and from C are equal, so \(AF = AD = 4 - x\) and \(CF = CE = 3 - x\).

\(AF + CF = AC\): \((4 - x) + (3 - x) = 5\), so \(x = 1\).

The radii OD and OE are perpendicular to AB and BC, \(\angle B = 90^\circ\) and \(OD = OE\), so ODBE is a square and the radius is \(OD = BD = 1\) cm.

(Alternatively, joining O to A, B and C splits the triangle into three triangles of height r: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = \dfrac{1}{2}r(4 + 3 + 5)\), so \(6 = 6r\) and \(r = 1\) cm.)

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the given figure, if a circle touches the side QR of \(\Delta PQR\) at S and extended sides PQ and PR at M and N respectively, then prove that : \(PM = \dfrac{1}{2}(PQ + QR + PR)\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - triangle PQR with the circle touching QR at S and the extended sides PQ and PR at M and N; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
Tangents drawn to a circle from an external point are equal, so

\(PM = PN\) (from P), \(QM = QS\) (from Q), \(RN = RS\) (from R).

Now \(PM = PQ + QM\) and \(PN = PR + RN\), so

\(2PM = PM + PN = PQ + QM + PR + RN = PQ + QS + PR + RS\)

\(= PQ + (QS + SR) + PR = PQ + QR + PR\).

So \(PM = \dfrac{1}{2}(PQ + QR + PR)\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A solid is in the form of a cylinder with hemispherical ends. The total height of the solid is 20 cm and the diameter of the cylinder is 7 cm. Find the total volume of the solid. \(\left(\text{Use } \pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\)
rows.solution:
The radius of the cylinder and of each hemisphere is \(\dfrac{7}{2}\) cm. The two hemispherical ends take up \(\dfrac{7}{2} + \dfrac{7}{2} = 7\) cm of the height, so the cylinder is \(20 - 7 = 13\) cm high.

Total volume \(= \pi r^2 h + 2 \times \dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3 = \pi r^2\left(h + \dfrac{4}{3}r\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times \left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^2 \times \left(13 + \dfrac{14}{3}\right) = \dfrac{77}{2} \times \dfrac{53}{3} = \dfrac{4081}{6}\) cm\(^3 \approx 680.17\) cm\(^3\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem:
Two dice of different colours are thrown at the same time. Write down all the possible outcomes. What is the probability that :

(i) same number appears on both the dice ?

(ii) different number appears on both the dice ?

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: Determine graphically, the coordinates of vertices of a triangle whose equations are \(2x - 3y + 6 = 0\); \(2x + 3y - 18 = 0\) and \(x = 0\). Also, find the area of this triangle.
rows.solution:
Points on \(2x - 3y + 6 = 0\), that is \(y = \dfrac{2x + 6}{3}\):

| \(x\) | \(-3\) | 0 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 0 | 2 | 4 |

Points on \(2x + 3y - 18 = 0\), that is \(y = \dfrac{18 - 2x}{3}\):

| \(x\) | 0 | 3 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 6 | 4 | 0 |

The line \(x = 0\) is the y-axis.

Plot the points and draw the two lines on the same axes. They meet each other at \(B(3, 4)\); the first meets the y-axis at \(A(0, 2)\) and the second at \(C(0, 6)\).

The vertices of the triangle are \(A(0, 2)\), \(B(3, 4)\) and \(C(0, 6)\).

The side AC lies along the y-axis, of length \(6 - 2 = 4\) units, and the perpendicular from B to the y-axis has length 3 units (the x-coordinate of B).

Area of triangle ABC \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = 6\) square units.

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: A faster train takes one hour less than a slower train for a journey of 200 km. If the speed of the slower train is 10 km/hr less than that of the faster train, find the speeds of the two trains.
rows.solution:
Let the speed of the faster train be \(x\) km/h, so the slower train's speed is \((x - 10)\) km/h.

The faster train takes one hour less over 200 km:

\(\dfrac{200}{x - 10} - \dfrac{200}{x} = 1\), so \(\dfrac{2000}{x(x - 10)} = 1\) and \(x^2 - 10x - 2000 = 0\).

\((x - 50)(x + 40) = 0\), so \(x = 50\) (a speed cannot be negative, so \(x = -40\) is rejected).

The faster train travels at 50 km/h and the slower train at 40 km/h.

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: The sum of the areas of two squares is \(640\,\text{m}^2\). If the difference in their perimeters is 64 m, find the sides of the two squares.
rows.solution:
Let the sides of the two squares be \(x\) m and \(y\) m, with \(x > y\).

Sum of the areas: \(x^2 + y^2 = 640\). Difference of the perimeters: \(4x - 4y = 64\), so \(y = x - 16\).

Substituting: \(x^2 + (x - 16)^2 = 640\), so \(2x^2 - 32x + 256 = 640\), that is \(x^2 - 16x - 192 = 0\).

\((x - 24)(x + 8) = 0\), so \(x = 24\) (a length cannot be negative, so \(x = -8\) is rejected), and \(y = 24 - 16 = 8\).

The sides of the squares are 24 m and 8 m.

rows.stem: State and prove Basic Proportionality Theorem.
rows.solution:
Theorem (Basic Proportionality Theorem). If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.

Given: in triangle ABC, a line parallel to BC meets AB at D and AC at E. To prove: \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Construction: join BE and CD, and draw \(DM \perp AC\) and \(EN \perp AB\).

Proof: \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(BDE)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AD \cdot EN}{\frac{1}{2} DB \cdot EN} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}\), and \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(DEC)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AE \cdot DM}{\frac{1}{2} EC \cdot DM} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Triangles BDE and DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC, so \(\text{ar}(BDE) = \text{ar}(DEC)\). Hence \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

rows.stem:
In the given figure, CM and RN are respectively the medians of \(\Delta ABC\) and \(\Delta PQR\). If \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\), then prove that :

(i) \(\Delta AMC \sim \Delta PNR\)

(ii) \(\Delta CMB \sim \Delta RNQ\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - triangle ABC with median CM to AB and triangle PQR with median RN to PQ; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
\(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\), so their corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional. CM and RN are medians, so M is the mid-point of AB and N the mid-point of PQ: \(AB = 2AM = 2MB\) and \(PQ = 2PN = 2NQ\).

(i) \(\angle A = \angle P\), and \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{AC}{PR}\), that is \(\dfrac{2AM}{2PN} = \dfrac{AC}{PR}\), so \(\dfrac{AM}{PN} = \dfrac{AC}{PR}\).

In triangles AMC and PNR, the angles at A and P are equal and the sides including them are proportional. So by the SAS similarity criterion, \(\Delta AMC \sim \Delta PNR\).

(ii) \(\angle B = \angle Q\), and \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR}\), that is \(\dfrac{2MB}{2NQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR}\), so \(\dfrac{MB}{NQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR}\).

In triangles CMB and RNQ, the angles at B and Q are equal and the sides including them are proportional. So by the SAS similarity criterion, \(\Delta CMB \sim \Delta RNQ\).

rows.stem:
The mean of the following frequency distribution is 35. Find the values of \(x\) and \(y\), if the sum of frequencies is 25 :

| Class | Frequency |
|---|---|
| 0-10 | 1 |
| 10-20 | \(x\) |
| 20-30 | 5 |
| 30-40 | 7 |
| 40-50 | \(y\) |
| 50-60 | 3 |
| 60-70 | 1 |
What is the distance covered to pick up the first potato and drop it in bucket ?
rows.context:
In a potato race, a bucket is placed at the starting point, which is 5 m from the first potato. The other potatoes are arranged 3 m apart in a straight line, with a total of 10 potatoes, as shown in the figure :

A competitor starts from the bucket, picks up the nearest potato, runs back to the bucket to drop it in, then returns to pick up the next potato. This process continues until all the potatoes are in the bucket.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the bucket and the row of ten potatoes with the gaps marked; every distance is in the passage. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
The first potato is 5 m from the bucket. The competitor runs 5 m to it and 5 m back to the bucket.

Distance \(= 5 + 5 = 10\) m.

rows.stem: What is the distance covered to pick up the second potato and drop it in bucket ?
rows.context:
In a potato race, a bucket is placed at the starting point, which is 5 m from the first potato. The other potatoes are arranged 3 m apart in a straight line, with a total of 10 potatoes, as shown in the figure :

A competitor starts from the bucket, picks up the nearest potato, runs back to the bucket to drop it in, then returns to pick up the next potato. This process continues until all the potatoes are in the bucket.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The second potato is 3 m beyond the first, so it is \(5 + 3 = 8\) m from the bucket. The competitor runs 8 m to it and 8 m back.

Distance \(= 8 + 8 = 16\) m.

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: What is the total distance the competitor has to run ?
rows.context:
In a potato race, a bucket is placed at the starting point, which is 5 m from the first potato. The other potatoes are arranged 3 m apart in a straight line, with a total of 10 potatoes, as shown in the figure :

A competitor starts from the bucket, picks up the nearest potato, runs back to the bucket to drop it in, then returns to pick up the next potato. This process continues until all the potatoes are in the bucket.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The potatoes are 5 m, 8 m, 11 m, ... from the bucket, and each one needs a run there and back. So the distances for the 10 potatoes are 10 m, 16 m, 22 m, ..., an AP with \(a = 10\), \(d = 6\) and \(n = 10\).

Total distance \(= S_{10} = \dfrac{10}{2}[2 \times 10 + 9 \times 6] = 5 \times 74 = 370\) m.

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: If average speed of competitor is 5 m/s, then find the average time taken by competitor to put all the potatoes in the bucket.
rows.context:
In a potato race, a bucket is placed at the starting point, which is 5 m from the first potato. The other potatoes are arranged 3 m apart in a straight line, with a total of 10 potatoes, as shown in the figure :

A competitor starts from the bucket, picks up the nearest potato, runs back to the bucket to drop it in, then returns to pick up the next potato. This process continues until all the potatoes are in the bucket.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The run for each potato is there and back, so the distances are 10 m, 16 m, 22 m, ..., an AP with \(a = 10\), \(d = 6\) and \(n = 10\) potatoes.

Total distance \(= S_{10} = \dfrac{10}{2}[2 \times 10 + 9 \times 6] = 5 \times 74 = 370\) m.

At an average speed of 5 m/s, the time taken \(= \dfrac{370}{5} = 74\) seconds.

rows.stem: Find the length of the wire from the point ‘O’ to the top of section ‘B’.
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two sections ‘A’ and ‘B’. Tower is supported by wires from a point ‘O’ (as shown in figure).

Distance between the base of the tower and point ‘O’ is 6 m. From point ‘O’, the angle of elevation of the top of the section ‘B’ is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of section ‘A’ is \(60^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the tower with points P, B and A on it, the wires OB and OA and the two angles at O; every value is in the passage. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Let P be the base of the tower, so \(OP = 6\) m and \(\angle BOP = 30^\circ\), with \(\angle OPB = 90^\circ\).

In right triangle OPB, \(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{OP}{OB}\), so \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{6}{OB}\).

\(OB = \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{3}} = 4\sqrt{3}\) m.

rows.stem: Find the length of the wire from the point ‘O’ to the top of section ‘A’.
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two sections ‘A’ and ‘B’. Tower is supported by wires from a point ‘O’ (as shown in figure).

Distance between the base of the tower and point ‘O’ is 6 m. From point ‘O’, the angle of elevation of the top of the section ‘B’ is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of section ‘A’ is \(60^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the tower drawing; every value is in the passage. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Let P be the base of the tower, so \(OP = 6\) m and \(\angle AOP = 60^\circ\), with \(\angle OPA = 90^\circ\).

In right triangle OPA, \(\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{OP}{OA}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{6}{OA}\) and \(OA = 12\) m.

rows.stem: Find the distance AB.
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two sections ‘A’ and ‘B’. Tower is supported by wires from a point ‘O’ (as shown in figure).

Distance between the base of the tower and point ‘O’ is 6 m. From point ‘O’, the angle of elevation of the top of the section ‘B’ is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of section ‘A’ is \(60^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the tower drawing, labelling the tops of the two sections A and B; the passage gives every value. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Let P be the base of the tower, with \(OP = 6\) m.

In right triangle OPB, \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{BP}{OP}\), so \(BP = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{3}} = 2\sqrt{3}\) m.

In right triangle OPA, \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{AP}{OP}\), so \(AP = 6\sqrt{3}\) m.

\(AB = AP - BP = 6\sqrt{3} - 2\sqrt{3} = 4\sqrt{3}\) m.

rows.stem: Find the area of \(\Delta OPB\).
rows.context:
Radio towers are used for transmitting a range of communication services including radio and television. The tower will either act as an antenna itself or support one or more antennas on its structure. On a similar concept, a radio station tower was built in two sections ‘A’ and ‘B’. Tower is supported by wires from a point ‘O’ (as shown in figure).

Distance between the base of the tower and point ‘O’ is 6 m. From point ‘O’, the angle of elevation of the top of the section ‘B’ is \(30^\circ\) and the angle of elevation of the top of section ‘A’ is \(60^\circ\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - P, a vertex of the triangle OPB, is named only in the drawing; the passage speaks only of the base of the tower. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
P is the base of the tower, so triangle OPB is right-angled at P with \(OP = 6\) m and \(\angle BOP = 30^\circ\).

\(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{BP}{OP}\), so \(BP = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{3}} = 2\sqrt{3}\) m.

Area of triangle OPB \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times BP \times OP = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2\sqrt{3} \times 6 = 6\sqrt{3}\) m\(^2\).

rows.stem: What is the radius of circle ?
rows.context:
A brooch is crafted from silver wire in the shape of a circle with a diameter of 35 cm. The wire is also used to create 5 diameters, dividing the circle into 10 equal sectors as shown in figure.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - a circle divided by five diameters into ten equal sectors; every value is in the passage. Page idx 14.
rows.solution: The radius is half the diameter: \(r = \dfrac{35}{2} = 17.5\) cm.

rows.stem: What is the circumference of the brooch ?
rows.context:
A brooch is crafted from silver wire in the shape of a circle with a diameter of 35 cm. The wire is also used to create 5 diameters, dividing the circle into 10 equal sectors as shown in figure.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The diameter is 35 cm, so \(r = \dfrac{35}{2}\) cm.

Circumference \(= 2\pi r = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{35}{2} = 110\) cm.

rows.stem: What is the total length of silver wire required ?
rows.context:
A brooch is crafted from silver wire in the shape of a circle with a diameter of 35 cm. The wire is also used to create 5 diameters, dividing the circle into 10 equal sectors as shown in figure.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The wire makes the circle and the 5 diameters. The circumference is \(2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{35}{2} = 110\) cm, and each diameter is 35 cm.

Total length of wire \(= 110 + 5 \times 35 = 110 + 175 = 285\) cm.

rows.stem: What is the area of each sector of the brooch ?
rows.context:
A brooch is crafted from silver wire in the shape of a circle with a diameter of 35 cm. The wire is also used to create 5 diameters, dividing the circle into 10 equal sectors as shown in figure.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The 10 equal sectors share \(360^\circ\), so each has a central angle of \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{10} = 36^\circ\). The radius is \(\dfrac{35}{2}\) cm.

Area of each sector \(= \dfrac{36}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{35}{2} \times \dfrac{35}{2} = \dfrac{385}{4} = 96.25\) cm\(^2\).
